reason: The except tuple (TimeoutError, McpError, OSError) is narrower than the docstring promises, but the headline consequence is disproved by a real kill/restart experiment: when the MCP server dies the SDK surfaces the in-flight call as McpError (60 s read timeout / CONNECTION_CLOSED), which IS caught, the session is dropped, and after the server restarts the next call succeeds - no 'cached until app restart'. The real defect is different: a dead child costs a full 60 s stall on the first call, and the call after that raised asyncio.CancelledError ('Cancelled via cancel scope' from the dead transport's task group) which escapes _call_tool's `except Exception` as a non-ProviderError, so the registry does not fall through to yfinance for that request.
evidence_checked: Read McpClient, the provider's _call_tool, and the installed mcp 1.27.1 transport/session error paths; ran the real McpClient against a local FastMCP server I started, killed and restarted (each call in its own task, as FastAPI requests are).
repro_check: /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-lokavyasingh-Documents-dev-vysted-terminal/3e7ae14d-d48a-4882-8a75-f7608754c23f/scratchpad/refute-mcp/drive2.py: 1-live OK; 2-dead McpError 'Timed out ... 60.0 seconds' session dropped (60.0 s); 3-dead-again CancelledError session None; 4-restarted OK; 5-restarted OK. (Same-task variant drive.py: every call CancelledError - an artefact of reusing the opener task, not production.)

reason: The swallow-to-empty is real (list_agents/list_workflows/list_runs map any httpx.HTTPError to an empty list), but the trigger is mis-stated: in production bind_app is always called so the tools use the in-process ASGITransport and the 127.0.0.1:0 fallback is unreachable; the actual path is a 5xx from the in-process route -> raise_for_status HTTPStatusError (an HTTPError) -> confident empty list. The three bare raise_for_status sites do not escape as raw transport errors either - FastMCP/lowlevel server convert a raising tool into an isError=True result. A rare in-process 5xx is a medium, not high, silent degradation.

repro_check: Code-level: force GET /agents to 500 in-process -> list_agents returns {'agents': []}; not run live (non-GET tools/call needs vy.py and a way to break the route).

reason: The race cannot occur under asyncio: _open assigns _session and bumps _generation with no await between them, and _ensure_session reads the pair in one expression with no await after the lock is released, so no sibling coroutine can interleave a torn (session, generation) read; close() re-checks the generation under the lock, and McpClient is never driven from another thread or loop (no asyncio.run / run_coroutine_threadsafe in services/routers/agents). The assert can never fire (either the session was non-None, or _open set it or raised).
evidence_checked: Read _open/_ensure_session/close; grepped services/, routers/, agents/ for cross-thread event-loop use (none).
repro_check: Code-level: no suspension point exists between the two attribute writes or the two attribute reads; cooperative scheduling makes both atomic.

reason: The two threads only touch the environment through std::env::set_var/remove_var, and std's own env functions are mutually synchronised: the std docs define the unsafety as other threads reading/writing the environment 'through functions or global variables other than the ones in this module'. The spawn threads' other env-adjacent work does not go through libc getenv (wait_for_port connects to ('127.0.0.1', port), a literal IP parse with no DNS lookup). The remaining hazard (a C library in another Tauri/webview thread calling getenv) is generic to any set_var after setup starts and is not removed by the proposed fix. I could not open the std source itself (network reset); this rests on the published std contract.

repro_check: Docs + code: both writers use std::env (mutually locked); no libc env reader identified on either spawn thread.
